Analog Devices engineer senses the world for the better

     INNOVATION Dr Helen Berney, senior process design engineer at Analog Devices. Image: Nick Bradshaw/DCU

  Dr Helen Berney from Analog Devices combines her skills to improve how we can sense the world with engineering. She spoke to Claire O’Connell.

  Life is busy and fast, so how do you find opportunities along the way? By watching out for them, and by being willing to learn. 

  That approach has served Dr Helen Berney well throughout her career and now, as a senior process design engineer at Analog Devices , she is looking to new ways to find signals in the noise. 

  That’s because Analog, a global multinational that recently celebrated 40 years in Limerick, makes electronic devices that can sense and process signals. 

  As a business-to-business company, Analog might not be a household name, but its technology is embedded in devices in consumer devices such as phones and fridges, and across industries including healthcare, agri-food, aerospace, automotive and the internet of things. 

  “We take analogue signals and translate them into the digital world and then back again,” said Berney, who has worked with the company for more than a decade. 

 Her role at Analog started as their representative in the Biomedical Diagnostics Institute (BDI) in Dublin City University (DCU), a centre funded by Science Foundation Ireland to explore new platforms to detect or monitor sign

 Another learning from the academic-industry partnership was how to convert research findings into innovations that could be used by industry. “I came from academia and I worked on projects with an industrial slant, but, until you come into industry, [you] don’t realise the gap between having a magnificently elegant concept and industry’s need to make a product at scale.” 

  “Analog does really great outreach, we are involved in Limerick for Engineering and we present at the BT Young Scientist & Technology Exhibition every year.”

##### Company Overview

Analog Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ: ADI) is a global semiconductor company specializing in the design, manufacture, and marketing of a broad portfolio of high-performance analog, mixed-signal, and digital signal processing (DSP) integrated circuits (ICs). Founded in 1965 and headquartered in Wilmington, Massachusetts (with major engineering operations in Wilmington and Norwood, Massachusetts, as well as significant global design centers), ADI serves a diverse set of end markets including industrial automation, communications infrastructure, automotive, and consumer electronics. The company operates primarily as a fabless or fab-lite semiconductor manufacturer, leveraging both internal fabrication facilities and third-party foundries to produce its products.

ADI's product portfolio spans data converters (analog-to-digital and digital-to-analog converters), amplifiers, power management ICs, radio frequency (RF) and microwave components, MEMS (microelectromechanical systems) sensors, and embedded processing solutions. Among its most recognized and commercially significant products are the AD9361 RF Agile Transceiver, widely used in software-defined radio and wireless infrastructure; the ADXL345 MEMS accelerometer, a benchmark product in motion sensing; and the AD7124-8 precision ADC, used extensively in industrial measurement applications. ADI also produces the ADuM series digital isolators and the LTC6811 battery stack monitor, a critical component in electric vehicle (EV) battery management systems. Following its acquisition of Maxim Integrated in 2021, ADI significantly expanded its power management and embedded security product lines.
